Known from early medieval carved stones, this people lived north of the Firth of Forth before merging with Dál Riata to form the Kingdom of Alba — who were they?
Picts: Medieval tribal confederation in northern Britain.
He ascended a throne at age two in 1908, then later reigned as a puppet emperor for a wartime Japanese state and was held as a war criminal until 1959 — which last emperor of China is he?
Puyi: Emperor of China (1908–1912) and of Manchukuo (1934–1945)
This centuries-long string of campaigns by northern Iberian Christian kingdoms drew to a close in 1492 with the fall of Granada, ending all Muslim rule on the peninsula — by what name is it known?
The eldest son of a U.S. president assassinated in 1865, this lawyer was the only one of his parents' four children to live past 18, and later served as Secretary of War — who is he?
Robert Todd Lincoln: American lawyer and politician (1843–1926)
A key figure in Japan's Meiji Restoration, this samurai later led a doomed 1877 uprising against the very government he helped create, dying in the fighting — who was he?
Saigō Takamori: Japanese samurai and politician (1828–1877)
A billionaire businessman who studied economics at Harvard, this politician served two separate terms as president of Chile between 2010 and 2022 — who was he?
Emulating the medieval chevauchée, this scorched-earth 1864 Civil War campaign cut from Atlanta to the captured port of Savannah. What was it called?
Sherman's March to the Sea: 1864 military campaign of the American Civil War.

Considered erotic poetry unlike other biblical books, this text narrates a passionate dialogue between a woman and her lover, warning the 'daughters of Jerusalem' not to awaken love too soon — what is it?
Song of Songs: Book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament.
Nicknamed the 'Tiger King' for his ferocity, this 29th monarch of the Ayutthaya Kingdom is credited with devising the fundamental techniques of Muay Thai — who is he?
This Aztec god of the night sky, hurricanes, and conflict had the jaguar as his animal double, and his main festival involved ritual human sacrifice — who is he?
Tezcatlipoca: Aztec deity of darkness and violence.
A former Army officer, this Arkansas Republican unseated incumbent Mark Pryor in 2014 to become the state's junior U.S. senator — who is he?
Tom Cotton: American politician and veteran (born 1977)
The tenth monarch of Thailand's Chakri dynasty, he delayed his accession ceremony to mourn his late father — becoming, at 64, the oldest Thai king ever to take the throne. Who is he?
One of Stalin's closest allies, this Soviet foreign minister gave his name to an improvised firebomb still hurled at protests today — who was he?
Vyacheslav Molotov: Soviet politician and diplomat (1890–1986)
Born in June 1982 and heir apparent to the throne, he met his future wife while studying geography at St Andrews and later flew with an air ambulance service — who is he?
William, Prince of Wales: Heir apparent to the British throne (born 1982). William, Prince of Wales (William Arthur Philip Louis; born 21 June 1982), is the heir apparent to the British throne.
Born in the Khan Yunis refugee camp and educated at the Islamic University of Gaza, he rose to lead Hamas in Gaza before being killed in a 2024 clash with the IDF — who was he?
Yahya Sinwar: Palestinian militant and politician (1962–2024)
This ancient Iranian faith centers on the Avesta and reveres Ahura Mazda as the supreme, uncreated deity, teaching a struggle between Asha (truth) and Druj (the lie). What religion is it?
Zoroastrianism: Iranian religion founded by Zoroaster.
Who among these was born first?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Saint Valentine (born 175) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four came first?
Assembly language (founded 1949) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
David L. Hill is a physicist.
Which of these is a chemist?
Ellen Swallow Richards is a chemist. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
What is the atomic number of Nihonium?
Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.
What is the atomic number of Strontium?
Strontium is a chemical element; it has symbol Sr and atomic number 38.
In what year was Jensen Huang born?
Jensen Huang: The son of Taiwanese immigrants, Huang spent his childhood in Taiwan and Thailand before moving to the United States, where he was a student in Kentucky and Oregon.
In what year was Thomas Sowell born?
Thomas Sowell ( SOHL; born June 30, 1930) is an American economist, economic historian, and social theorist.
In what year was Adam Smith born?
Adam Smith: The work is notable for its contribution to economic theory, particularly in its exposition of the concept of absolute advantage.
In what year did Thomas Hobbes die?
Thomas Hobbes: Hobbes's academic journey began in Westport, leading him to the University of Oxford, where he was exposed to classical literature and mathematics.
In what year did Albert Einstein die?
Albert Einstein (14 March 1879 – 18 April 1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the known theory of relativity.
In what year was Chlorine discovered?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
Mikoyan MiG-35: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Marketed as a 4++ generation jet fighter, it is a further development of the MiG-29M/M2 and MiG-29K/KUB fighters.
Which country is HAL Tejas from?
HAL Tejas: India. The aircraft made its first flight in 2001 and entered into service with the IAF in 2015.
Who is credited with discovering Apus?
Apus: Petrus Plancius. Apus is a small constellation in the southern sky.
Who is credited with discovering Cat's Eye Nebula?
Cat's Eye Nebula: William Herschel. It is a well-studied object that has been observed from radio to X-ray wavelengths.
Who is credited with discovering Hydrogen?
Hydrogen: Henry Cavendish. Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
Who is credited with discovering Astatine?
Astatine: Emilio G. Segrè. Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.

While working at a Soviet computing centre in 1985, this engineer created one of history's most popular video games — yet earned no royalties from it until founding a company with Henk Rogers in 1996. Who is he?
Alexey Pajitnov (born April 16, 1955) is a Russian and American computer engineer and video game designer.
Named for the Portuguese word for indigo shrub, this simplest aromatic amine smells of rotten fish, ignites into a smoky flame, and is a key precursor to polyurethane and dyes — what compound is it?
Aniline (From) is an organic compound with the formula C6H5NH2.
This general medical term describes a joint disorder in which the smooth cartilage lining wears away, leaving bone to grind directly on bone during movement — what condition is it?
Arthritis is a general medical term used to describe a disorder in which the smooth cartilagenous layer that lines a joint is lost, resulting in bone grinding on bone during joint movement.
Marketed early on as the Debonair in its conventional-tail form, this piston single has been built continuously longer than any other aircraft ever made — which model?
Beechcraft Bonanza is an American general aviation aircraft introduced in 1947 by Beech Aircraft Corporation of Wichita, Kansas.

Native to eastern North America with resident populations as far north as Newfoundland, this crested songbird in the crow family has a black, U-shaped collar around its neck and a mostly white chest — name it?
Blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America.
This condition results from inflamed, fluid-filled sacs that cushion friction points between bones, tendons, and muscles, commonly striking the shoulder, elbow, hip, or knee — what is it?
Bursitis is the inflammation of one or more bursae in the body.
This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' and studies cell-surface sugars called glycans from her professorship at Stanford — who is she?
Carolyn Bertozzi (born October 10, 1966) is an American chemist and Nobel laureate, known for her wide-ranging work spanning both chemistry and biology.
Present naturally in breast milk and added to infant formula, this essential nutrient is also a building block for a neurotransmitter that controls muscle movement — which compound?
Choline is a cation with the chemical formula +.
This legless, non-venomous lizard native to Europe is often mistaken for a snake despite having smooth, non-overlapping scales and semi-fossorial burrowing habits — what is it called?
Common slow worm (Anguis fragilis) is a non-venomous species of legless lizard native to Europe.

Caused by prolonged exposure to glucocorticoids like cortisol, this collection of symptoms includes abdominal weight gain with thin limbs, a rounded red face, and weak, fragile skin that heals poorly — what's it called?
Cushing's syndrome is a collection of signs and symptoms due to prolonged exposure to glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

This is the practice of communication between representatives of states or institutions aimed at influencing international events, serving as the main instrument through which foreign policy goals are pursued. What is this practice called?
Diplomacy is the communication by representatives of state, intergovernmental, or non-governmental institutions intended to influence events in the international system.
This is the only surviving member of its order, the Proboscidea, and its tusks are actually overgrown incisor teeth used as both weapons and tools — what animal is it?
Elephant are the largest living land animals.
This Hungarian-American physicist won the 1963 Nobel for applying fundamental symmetry principles to the atomic nucleus, having once worked as an assistant to David Hilbert at Göttingen. Who was he?
Eugene Wigner (November 17, 1902 - January 1, 1995) was a Hungarian-American theoretical physicist who also contributed to mathematical physics.
Found at the terminal end of the limb in many vertebrates, this weight-bearing anatomical structure enables locomotion and is typically made up of multiple bony segments — what is it?
Foot (pl.: feet) is an anatomical structure found in many vertebrates. The plural form feet is an instance of i-mutation.
With the symbol Ge and atomic number 32, this lustrous, brittle metalloid was predicted to exist by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, decades before it was actually discovered — name this element?
Germanium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ge and atomic number 32.
A French polymath dabbling in anthropology, medicine and physics, he's best remembered for an 1895 book that became a seminal work of crowd psychology — who was he?
Gustave Le Bon (7 May 1841 - 13 December 1931) was a leading French polymath whose areas of interest included anthropology, psychology, sociology, medicine, invention, and physics.
Sometimes called urticaria, this itchy rash of raised welts can flare for minutes or days, may follow an allergy or infection, and in half of all cases has no identifiable cause — what is it?
Hives is a kind of skin rash with red or flesh-colored, raised, itchy bumps.

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.
This Canadian-American physical educator invented an entire sport, wrote its original rule book after moving to the United States, and founded the University of Kansas's program in 1898 — who is he?
James Naismith (November 6, 1861 - November 28, 1939) was a Canadian-American physical educator, physician, Christian chaplain, and sports coach, best known as the inventor of the game of basketball.
Endemic to New Caledonia's mountain forests, this bluish-grey, nearly flightless bird sports bright red legs and unique nasal corns shared by no other bird — what is it?
Kagu (Rhynochetos jubatus) is a crested, long-legged, and bluish-grey bird endemic to the dense mountain forests of New Caledonia.
Also known as Al-Kashi's theorem, which trigonometry rule relates the lengths of a triangle's three sides to the cosine of one of its angles?

Law of cosines (also known as the cosine formula or cosine rule or Al-Kashi's theorem) relates the lengths of the sides of a triangle to the cosine of one of its angles. The law of cosines is useful for solving a triangle when all three sides or two sides and their included angle are given.
Descended from the YF-22 prototype, this supersonic air-superiority stealth fighter saw Boeing build its wings and aft fuselage while the prime contractor handled final assembly — what is it?
Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor is an American twin-engine, jet-powered, all-weather, supersonic stealth fighter aircraft.

This psychiatric state of abnormally elevated energy and mood is sometimes called the mirror image of depression, though its heightened feelings can turn irritable or anxious just as easily as euphoric — what is it called?
Mania (also known as manic syndrome) is a psychiatric behavioral syndrome defined as a state of abnormally elevated arousal, affect, and energy level.
Discovered in 1893 and existing as two enantiomers, this CNS stimulant is best known in its hydrochloride salt form as 'crystal meth' — what is it?

Methamphetamine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant that is primarily used as a recreational or performance-enhancing drug and less commonly as a second-line treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
First synthesized in 2003 by Russian and American scientists at Dubna, this synthetic element — atomic number 115 — was named in 2016 for the oblast around its birthplace — what is it?
Moscovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mc and atomic number 115.
Found across North America, Europe, North Africa, and Asia, this three-stage amphibian passes through an aquatic larval phase and a land-dwelling 'eft' stage before adulthood — what is it?
Newt is a salamander in the subfamily Pleurodelinae.
Which applied-math discipline, born from pre-WWII military planning and overlapping heavily with industrial engineering, hunts for the maximum profit or minimum cost in real-world problems?

Operations research (British), often shortened to the initialism OR, is a branch of applied mathematics that deals with the development and application of analytical methods to improve management and decision-making.
Native to the islands of Southeast Asia, this bushy perennial herb in the mint family is prized for a fragrant essential oil used widely in perfumery — what plant is it?
Patchouli (also spelled patchouly or pachouli; Pogostemon cablin) is a species of flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, commonly called the mint or deadnettle family.
Its name comes from the Greek for 'love of wisdom,' and physics and psychology were once branches of it — what is this rational inquiry into existence and knowledge?

Philosophy (from Ancient Greek philosophia, lit. 'love of wisdom') is a systematic study of general and fundamental questions concerning topics like existence, knowledge, mind, reason, language, and value.

This category of polymers, most commonly known in the form of PET, is prized for clothing but — unlike some of its naturally occurring plant and insect cousins — rarely biodegrades — what material is it?
Polyester is a category of polymers that contain one or two ester linkages in every repeat unit of their main chain.
Its biological practitioners link it to neuroscience while its social scientists study groups, all in service of studying the mind and behavior — what is this academic discipline?
Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behavior. Psychology is an academic discipline of broad scope, crossing the boundaries between the natural and social sciences.

This condition, often triggered by crush injuries or extreme exercise, causes skeletal muscle to break down so rapidly that it can turn urine tea-colored and damage the kidneys — what condition is it?
Rhabdomyolysis (shortened as rhabdo) is a condition in which damaged skeletal muscle breaks down rapidly.
Named after an American veterinary surgeon, this genus of rod-shaped, gram-negative bacteria includes over 2,650 serotypes within a single major species — name it?
Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped, (bacillus) Gram-negative bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae.

Drawing on tools from anthropology, biology, medicine, psychology, and criminology, this scientific field studies human sexual interests, behaviors, and functions, distinct from purely social commentary on the subject — what is this field called?
Sexology is the scientific study of human sexuality, including human sexual interests, behaviors, and functions.
This use of the human voice for language ranges from informing and persuading to simply asking or declaring, combining vowels and consonants into meaningful words — what is it called?
Speech is the use of the human voice as a medium for language.
The only surviving tiger population in the Sunda Islands, found on the Indonesian island of Sumatra after its Bali and Javan cousins went extinct in the 20th century — what is it?
Sumatran tiger is a population of Panthera tigris sondaica on the Indonesian island of Sumatra.
This vast domain of human practice — divided into visual, literary, and performing branches — lets people transmit values, ideas, and experiences across generations. What is it?
The arts are a vast range of human practices involving creative expression, storytelling, and cultural participation.
Taken by mouth, injection, or inhalation, this steroid helps prevent asthma and COPD flare-ups from worsening — which medication?
Triamcinolone is a glucocorticoid used to treat certain skin diseases, allergies, and rheumatic disorders among others.
This southwestern European viper's bite can be more dangerous than the common adder's — up to 4% of untreated cases are fatal — which species?
Vipera aspis is a viper species found in southwestern Europe.
Passed only from fathers to sons, this genetic structure carries the SRY gene that typically triggers development of male gonads in mammals — what is it?
Y chromosome is one of two sex chromosomes in therian mammals and other organisms.
Genetic in roughly 80% of cases, this long-term skin condition clogs hair follicles with dead skin and sebum, producing blackheads and pimples on the face, chest, and back — what is it?
Acne: Skin condition characterized by pimples.

German-born theoretical physicist celebrated for E=mc² and work on relativity — he won the 1921 Nobel Prize not for those breakthroughs, but for discovering the photoelectric effect. Who revolutionized physics across multiple domains?
Commonly called buffalo, this large grazing mammal endemic to North America is one of just two living species in its genus, alongside a European cousin — what animal is it?
American bison: Species of bovid artiodactyl mammal.
Known in veterinary medicine as inappetence when it strikes cats, dogs, or cattle, which general medical term describes any loss of appetite — a symptom rather than a diagnosis in itself?
Anorexia (symptom): Loss of appetite. The symptom also occurs in non-human animals, such as cats, dogs, cattle, goats, and sheep.

Nicknamed for its resemblance to a stinging insect, this orb-weaver spider sports bold yellow, white, and black bands across Central and Northern Europe, parts of Asia and Africa, and even the Azores — what species is it?
Argiope bruennichi: Species of orb-weaver spider. Like many other members of the same genus Argiope, this species has distinctive yellow, white and black markings on its abdomen.
The famous AL 288-1 skeleton nicknamed 'Lucy,' unearthed in Ethiopia's Afar region, belongs to which extinct East African hominin species that lived roughly 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago?
Australopithecus afarensis: Extinct hominid from the Pliocene of East Africa.
This inflammatory condition causes recurring, painful mouth sores along with eye inflammation and arthritis, and is diagnosed after at least three sore outbreaks in a year — which condition?
Behçet's disease: Inflammatory disorder. Behçet's disease or Behçet's syndrome (BD; sometimes written Behcet) is a type of inflammatory disorder which affects multiple parts of the body.
This small Old World flycatcher breeds in rocky habitats from the British Isles to Morocco and central China, staying put in milder areas but migrating from colder ones — what bird is it?
Black redstart: Species of bird. The black redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros) is a small passerine bird in the Old World flycatcher family.
Formed from the C5-T1 spinal nerve roots, this network of nerves runs through the neck and over the first rib to supply the shoulder, arm, and hand — what is it?
Brachial plexus: Network of nerves. This plexus extends from the spinal cord, through the cervicoaxillary canal in the neck, over the first rib, and into the armpit.
Developed in 1964 at Britain's Royal Radar Establishment and influenced by JOVIAL, this programming language was chosen by the UK Ministry of Defence in 1971 for military applications — what is it?
CORAL: Early programming language. The R was originally for "radar", not "real-time".
Derived from Greek words for 'heart' and 'study,' this branch of internal medicine covers coronary artery disease, heart failure, and electrophysiology — which medical field?
Cardiology: Branch of medicine dealing with the heart.
Triggered by anything from a stroke to a bout of altitude sickness, this dangerous buildup of fluid inside the skull raises pressure on brain tissue and can cause seizures or worse — what is it?
Cerebral edema: Excess accumulation of fluid in the brain.
This class of jawed fish — including sharks, rays, skates, and ghost-like chimaeras — has skeletons made entirely of cartilage rather than bone — what is it called?
Chondrichthyes: Class of jawed cartilaginous fish. Chondrichthyes are aquatic vertebrates with paired fins, paired nares, placoid scales, and conus arteriosus in the heart.
Recognizable by a prominent crest and curved bill, this Australasian parrot family includes 21 species, the smallest of which is the cockatiel — which family of birds?
Cockatoo: Any bird in the family Cacatuidae.
What is this — “Animal sexual reproductive act in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body”?

Copulation (zoology): Animal sexual reproductive act in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body. In zoology, copulation is animal sexual behavior in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body, especially directly into the female's reproductive tract.
This medical sign turns the lips, nail beds, and ear lobes a bluish-purple hue when blood isn't carrying enough oxygen, and comes in central and peripheral forms — what is it called?
Cyanosis: Decreased oxygen in the blood. Cyanosis is apparent usually in the body tissues covered with thin skin, including the mucous membranes, lips, nail beds, and ear lobes.
Often called eczema, this term covers skin inflammation marked by itchiness, redness and rash — sometimes with tiny blisters, sometimes thickening over time. What is it?
Dermatitis: Inflammatory disease of the skin.

Developed in the early 1950s to replace the propeller-driven Skyraider, this US Navy carrier jet had a maximum takeoff weight of just 24,500 pounds — about half the Navy's specification — which aircraft?
Douglas A-4 Skyhawk: Carrier-based attack aircraft.
Linked with orgasm and involving involuntary pelvic-floor contractions, this male bodily process can even happen during sleep as a so-called 'wet dream' — what is it?
Ejaculation: Semen discharge from the male reproductive tract.
This 1939 Nobel Physics laureate invented the cyclotron and went on to found two national laboratories that carry his surname today — who was he?

Scientifically known as Chloris chloris, this small finch is widespread across Europe, North Africa, and Southwest Asia, and has also been introduced to Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Argentina — what bird is this?
European greenfinch: Species of bird. The European greenfinch or simply the greenfinch (Chloris chloris) is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae.
Also known as the bodhi tree, this species is revered in four South Asian religions as the tree beneath which Buddha is said to have reached enlightenment — which species?
Ficus religiosa: Species of fig. Ficus religiosa or sacred fig is a species of fig native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina that belongs to Moraceae, the fig or mulberry family.

One of the first management consultants, this American mechanical engineer wrote a 1909 book — later voted the most influential management book of the 20th century — and helped found industrial engineering. Who was he?
Frederick Winslow Taylor: American mechanical engineer (1856–1915)
Deriving its name from Greek words for 'earth' and 'study of', this branch of natural science examines rocks and the processes that have shaped the planet over time — what is it called?
Geology: Scientific study of Earth's physical composition.
This common name covers edible fruit from the Ribes genus — the same genus as currants — coming in colors from green and red to purple, yellow, white, or black — which fruit?
Gooseberry: Species of Ribes cultivated for its edible fruit.
Producing up to a hundred billion new cells a day from specialized stem cells, this biological process manufactures every component of blood — what is it?
Haematopoiesis: Formation of blood cellular components.
Often contracted from undercooked shellfish or contaminated water, this foodborne viral liver disease causes symptoms like jaundice and fever that typically last around eight weeks — what is it?
Hepatitis A: Acute infectious disease of the liver.
This hormone, produced by cells surrounding a growing embryo, is what's detected in pregnancy tests and sometimes secreted by tumors, aiding cancer diagnosis — what is it?
Human chorionic gonadotropin: Hormone for the maternal recognition of pregnancy.
Typically starting to work within an hour, this NSAID relieves pain, fever, and inflammation but can worsen asthma and, in later pregnancy, is considered harmful — which drug?

Credited with the oldest known systematic classification of chemical substances, this alchemist's corpus also contains the earliest instructions for deriving ammonium chloride from organic matter — who is he?
Jabir ibn Hayyan: Islamic alchemist and polymath (died c. 806–816)
Building his first firearm at age 13 in his father's gun shop, this American designer earned 128 patents and pioneered the autoloading pistol — who is he?
In this eye disorder, the cornea gradually thins and bulges into a cone shape, causing blurry or double vision often linked to excessive eye rubbing as a risk factor — which condition?
Keratoconus: Medical condition involving the eye.
Native to North America and infamous for occasionally eating their mates after reproduction, the females of this venomous spider species sport striking black-and-red coloring — what species is it?
Latrodectus mactans: Species of spider. Latrodectus mactans, known as southern black widow or simply black widow, and the shoe-button spider, is a venomous species of spider in the genus Latrodectus.
This big cat of the genus Panthera now ranges only in Sub-Saharan Africa and India, and is unusual among wild cats for living in social groups — what is it?
Lion: Large cat native to Africa and India.
Located near the backbone on either side of the heart, this organ extracts oxygen from the air and releases carbon dioxide, driven mainly by the diaphragm — which organ is it?
Lung: Primary organ of the respiratory system.
This sugar alcohol pulls double duty as a low-calorie sweetener and a drug given by injection to lower pressure in the eyes or inside the skull — an osmotic diuretic. What is it?
Native to Indomalaya and Australasia, this deciduous member of the mahogany family goes by names like chinaberry tree and Persian lilac — what is it?
Succeeding the Castro brothers, this engineer became Cuba's first head of state in nearly six decades who wasn't a member of that family — who is he?
Miguel Díaz-Canel: Leader of Cuba since 2021.
Sold under the brand name Singulair, this asthma medication blocks leukotriene D4 in the lungs but received a UK black box warning in 2019 over neuropsychiatric side effects — what is it?
Montelukast: Medication used in asthma or COPD.
Made of the same tough protein as claws, hooves, and horns, this protective plate covers the tip of your fingers and toes — what is it?
Nail (anatomy): Hard keratin protection of digit.
Sold under the brand name Macrobid, this antibacterial drug treats lower urinary tract infections but isn't effective against kidney infections. What is it?
Nitrofurantoin: Antibacterial drug. Nitrofurantoin, sold under the brand name Macrobid among others, is an antibacterial medication of the nitrofuran class.
First described in 1689 by a local naturalist, this aquatic cave-dwelling salamander is the only exclusively cave-dwelling chordate native to Europe — what is it?
Britain, Germany, and Italy jointly built this twin-engine, variable-sweep-wing combat jet through a tri-national consortium, first flying it in 1974 — which aircraft?
Panavia Tornado: Family of multi-role combat aircraft.
This psychiatric paraphilia involves a primary or exclusive sexual attraction to prepubescent children, with diagnostic criteria extending the cutoff age to thirteen — which disorder?
Pedophilia: Sexual attraction to prepubescent children. The DSM requires the arousal pattern must be present for 6 months or longer, while the ICD lacks this requirement.
This branch of linguistics studies how spoken languages organize meaningful sound units — the kind of contrast that separates 'bat' from 'gnat' — what field is it?
Phonology: Study of sound organization in languages.
Its name comes from the Greek for 'making,' and it leans on devices like assonance, alliteration, and metre to evoke meanings beyond the literal — what literary art is this?

Detected by receptors in your muscles, tendons, and joints, this sense tells your brain where your body is in space, working alongside vision and balance to keep you upright and coordinated — what's it called?
Proprioception: Sense of self-movement, force, and body position.
Found in notable amounts in capers, red onions, and kale, this bitter-tasting plant flavonol is a popular ingredient in dietary supplements — what compound?
Quercetin: Chemical compound. It is found in many fruits, vegetables, leaves, seeds, and grains; capers, red onions, and kale are common foods containing appreciable amounts of it.
Often compared to the film in a camera, this innermost, light-sensitive layer of the eye sends signals along the optic nerve to the visual cortex — what is it?
Retina: Part of the eye. The retina (from Latin rete 'net'; pl. retinae or retinas) is the innermost, light-sensitive layer of tissue of the eye.
Discovered in 1973 by Ruth Bishop via electron micrograph images, this fecal-oral pathogen is the leading cause of diarrheal illness in infants worldwide — which pathogen?
Rotavirus: Specific genus of RNA viruses.
Found in every ocean but never in fresh water, most of these bivalves can swim in rapid bursts across the seafloor rather than staying put — which shellfish?
Scallop: Family of shellfish, many edible.
Until 2010, this onion relative was classified as its own species before being folded back into the common onion — what is it?
Known commonly as chlorine bleach when dissolved in water, this unstable inorganic compound decomposes to release chlorine gas — what is it?
Sodium hypochlorite: Chemical compound. Sodium hypochlorite is an alkaline inorganic chemical compound with the formula NaOCl (also written as NaClO).
Famous for kite-shaped plates along its back and spikes on its tail, this Late Jurassic herbivore may have been preyed on by Allosaurus — which dinosaur?
Stegosaurus: Genus of Late Jurassic armored dinosaur.
Time named this marine biologist its first "Hero for the Planet" in 1998, the same year she became a National Geographic Explorer — and she'd already been NOAA's first chief scientist. Who is she?
Sylvia Earle: American marine biologist and lecturer.
Developed under the codename 'WhiteStar' and unveiled in Hawthorne, California in 2009, this full-size electric sedan won Motor Trend's Car of the Year in 2013 — which car?
Tesla Model S: Battery-electric full-size car. The Tesla Model S is a battery-electric, four-door full-size car that was produced by the American automaker Tesla from 2012 to 2026.
With the symbol Sn and atomic number 50, this metal emits a crackling 'cry' when bent and boasts more stable isotopes than any other element — which one?
Tin: Chemical element with atomic number 50 (Sn). A metallic-gray metal, tin is soft enough to be cut with little force, and a bar of tin can be bent by hand with little effort.

Once grimly nicknamed the "white death" and historically called consumption, this contagious bacterial disease usually starts in the lungs — and most who carry it never show a single symptom. What is it?
Tuberculosis: Infectious disease. Tuberculosis initially infects the lungs, but it can also spread to other parts of the body.
This glycopeptide antibiotic is given intravenously for MRSA infections like endocarditis and meningitis, but taken orally - where it's poorly absorbed - to treat a common gut infection - which drug?

Lukoil is a Russian multinational energy corporation headquartered in Moscow, specializing in the business of extraction, production, transport, and sale of petroleum, natural gas, petroleum products, and electricity.

Founded in 1895 in Wattens, Tyrol, this Austrian luxury goods conglomerate is famed worldwide for its cut crystal glass, alongside jewellery, watches, and optical instruments — what's the company called?
Swarovski is an Austrian luxury goods conglomerate that designs, manufactures, distributes and sells jewellery, watches and glass.
This Italian open-source company (now owned by Qualcomm) designs single-board microcontrollers and kits beloved by tinkerers building digital devices — what is it?
Arduino: Italian open-source hardware and software company.
Founded in 1919 and now owned by Stellantis, this French automaker made its name in 1934 with the Traction Avant, the world's first mass-produced car of its kind — what's the brand?
Citroën: French car brand of Stellantis. Citroën (French: [sitʁɔɛn]) is a French automobile brand owned by Stellantis since 2021.
Owned by AB InBev, this Mexican brewery exports Corona and Pacífico worldwide, and saw its flagship domestic beer overtake Bud Light as America's top seller by dollar sales in 2023 — which brewery?
Grupo Modelo: Large Mexican brewery. Grupo Modelo is a large brewery in Mexico owned by Anheuser-Busch InBev that exports beer to most countries of the world.
Registered in Paris and headquartered in Clichy, this firm owned 36 brands and 497 patents and ranks as the world's largest cosmetics company — which one?
L'Oréal: French multinational cosmetics and beauty company.
Backed by Oppo and co-founded in 2013 by Pete Lau and Carl Pei, this Shenzhen-based smartphone maker later saw Pei leave to found Nothing — which company?
Founded by Tokuji Hayakawa in 1912 and headquartered in Sakai, Osaka, this Japanese electronics maker has been majority-owned by Foxconn since 2016 — which company?
Sharp Corporation: Japanese electronics company. Sharp's net sales reached 2.55 trillion yen in fiscal year 2022 (ending 29 February 2024), according to Statista.

Headquartered in Vilnius, this Lithuanian company runs Europe's leading peer-to-peer marketplace for second-hand fashion, with sister arms in logistics, payments, and green investing — which platform?
Vinted: Lithuanian online-marketplace company. Vinted Group UAB is a Lithuanian technology company best known for its online marketplace Vinted.
